title: House Robber II
prompt: This is an extension of the classic house robber problem: the houses are now arranged in a circle, meaning the first house and the last house are adjacent to each other. Given `nums` where `nums[i]` is the money at house i, return the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses (remembering that house 0 and house n-1 count as adjacent).

examples.explanation: Robbing house 0 and house 2 is not allowed since they're adjacent in the circle, so the best is robbing just house 1 (money = 3).
Rob house 0 (1) and house 2 (3): total = 4. They aren't adjacent since house 3 sits between house 2 and house 0 in the circle.
All three houses are mutually adjacent in a circle of 3, so you can rob at most one; the best single house is 3.

hints: The circular constraint only really matters for the pairing of house 0 and house n-1. If you could ignore the circle, this would be the standard linear house robber problem.

Split into two cases: either house 0 is never robbed (consider houses 1..n-1 as a line), or house n-1 is never robbed (consider houses 0..n-2 as a line). At least one of these two cases must reflect the true optimum, since you can never legally rob both endpoints.

Run the standard linear house-robber DP (O(1) space, two rolling variables) on each of the two sub-arrays, and return the max of the two results. Handle the n=1 edge case separately since there's no 'exclude one end' array left.

solution.approach: Because houses 0 and n-1 are adjacent in the circle, any valid selection either excludes house 0 or excludes house n-1 (it can never include both). So compute the standard linear house-robber result on nums[0:n-1] (excluding the last house) and on nums[1:n] (excluding the first house), and return the max of the two. Use the O(1)-space rolling-variable version of linear house robber as a helper. Special-case n == 1 since slicing would otherwise produce an empty array for one of the two cases.
